UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
)

Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE, PROTEST,  
AND REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF  
PPL ELECTRIC UTILITIES CORPORATION 
Pursuant to Rules 211,1 212,2 and 2143 of the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission’s (“FERC” or the “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, PPL Electric 
Utilities Corporation (“PPL Electric”) respectfully moves to intervene in the above-captioned 
proceeding, provides the following protest (“Protest”), and requests clarification regarding 
PJM Interconnection L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) Filing.4 
PPL Electric greatly appreciates the work of the PJM Board and staff in acting to 
address the unique operational, planning, and markets challenges presented by large loads in 
the PJM Region,5 and PPL Electric remains committed to working towards an enduring 
connect and manage framework to “meet the moment.”6  It is in this collaborative spirit that

Registry, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (Aug. 13, 2026) (hereafter, the “IRAS Filing”).

(“Operating Agreement”), and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load-Serving Entities in the PJM 
Region (“RAA”).  Each of these Governing Agreements is currently located under PJM’s “Intra-PJM Tariffs” 
eTariff title, available here: https://etariff.ferc.gov/TariffBrowser.aspx?tid=1731.

to be cavalier and dodge the urgent need to meet the moment.”).

2 
PPL Electric submits this protest to highlight for the Commission a core reality of the IRAS 
Filing—it is not legally durable on appeal.   
As explained below, because of how PJM has drafted its Tariff language, if accepted 
without modification, the IRAS Filing would mark the first time in history that the Commission 
would be requiring the mandatory and involuntary designation of end-use retail customers 
(Eligible New Large Loads) to provide a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service (IRAS), 
and the compulsory provision of that FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service (IRAS) to a 
Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) pursuant to FERC-approved rates, terms, and 
conditions in a FERC-approved tariff.  While PJM correctly, and consistent with current 
process, defers to the applicable Electric Distributor and state/local regulatory authorities in 
determining which specific individual Eligible New Large Loads within a given zone should 
actually provide IRAS when called upon, the fact remains that all Eligible New Large Loads 
(end-use, retail customers) within a zone are assigned responsibility by PJM to provide this 
wholesale rate service, pursuant to FERC-jurisdictional rates, terms, and conditions, and must 
provide this wholesale rate service to PJM when called upon.  This exceeds the Commission’s 
legal authority under the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), under the plain language of the statute 
and applicable precedents.   
PPL Electric agrees with Chairman Swett on the need to create “legally durable”7 
solutions in this space.  Because PJM has provided the Commission with broad NRG 
 
7 Id. at Swett Concurrence, P 3 (“I wholeheartedly, fully concur with these orders, which we carefully crafted to 
execute upon the problems the Secretary identified in a manner that is quick, efficient, and legally durable.”).

3 
flexibility8 in this FPA section 2059 proceeding, PPL Electric offers two alternative routes that 
the Commission could take to ameliorate the jurisdictional challenges for the IRAS initiative.   
Option 1 -  
Have PJM’s Tariff language stop at the issuance of the 
Operating Instruction to Electric Distributors to curtail load, and 
leave the rates, terms, and conditions of that load curtailment 
service to state and local regulatory authorities—many of whom 
have already signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.  This 
would avoid a scenario where federally imposed obligations are 
colliding with state and local-jurisdictional law and tariffs, 
including the statutory “obligation to serve,” and would provide 
a much more jurisdictionally sound legal pathway to effectuate 
connect and manage under FPA section 201.   
Option 2 - 
Alternatively, make IRAS a voluntary FERC-jurisdictional 
service, whereby Electric Distributors and/or large load 
customers themselves can voluntarily choose to participate like 
any other wholesale market service provider in PJM (including 
demand response providers).  Given the enthusiasm with which 
many large load developers and Electric Distributors have 
signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge,10 there should clearly 
be a high level of interest in voluntarily participating in such a 
program.  Such a program would also be consistent with EPSA,11 
where the Supreme Court affirmed the Commission’s ability to 
create programs that “lure,” rather than force, end-use retail

in the event the Commission deems it necessary, and to help facilitate the Commission’s acceptance of this filing 
without delay, PJM provides notice that it consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or

and reasonable and act together to advance important resource adequacy objectives, they may also be considered 
discretely.”).

4 
customers into participating in FERC-jurisdictional wholesale 
markets. 
Beyond this, PPL Electric also highlights below several structural deficiencies in the 
IRAS Filing and respectfully requests that the Commission reject or modify these components, 
consistent with PJM’s NRG invitation. 
Finally, PPL Electric respectfully requests that PJM and/or the Commission clarify in 
this proceeding several important policy and implementation details of the IRAS Filing.  
I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
PPL Electric respectfully moves to intervene in the above-captioned proceeding.  PPL 
Electric is a Pennsylvania corporation and a wholly owned subsidiary of PPL Corporation.  
PPL Electric is an owner of transmission facilities in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), 
distributes electricity to all retail customers within its service territory in central and eastern 
Pennsylvania, and is a provider of last resort under Pennsylvania’s Electricity Generation 
Customer Choice and Competition Act, 66 Pa.C.S.A. § 2801, et seq.  PPL Electric is a 
designated Load Serving Entity in PJM, and a signatory to the PJM Consolidated Transmission 
Owners Agreement (“CTOA”) and the RAA. 
On August 13, 2026, PJM initiated the above-captioned FPA section 205 proceeding 
by submitting proposed Tariff and RAA revisions to establish IRAS—a service to be 
implemented by PJM during periods when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet 
demand in real time operations. 
Given the direct nexus between the IRAS Filing and PPL Electric’s roles and 
responsibilities within the PJM Region, PPL Electric has a direct, substantial, and independent 
interest in this proceeding, which no other party can adequately represent, and respectfully

5 
requests that the Commission grant this motion to intervene and that PPL Electric be afforded 
all the rights of a party to this proceeding. 
II. 
PROTEST 
A. PJM’s Proposal Unlawfully Requires the Mandatory and Involuntary Designation 
of End-Use Retail Customers (Eligible New Large Loads) to Provide a FERC-
Jurisdictional Wholesale Rate Service (IRAS), and the Compulsory Provision of 
that FERC-Jurisdictional Wholesale Rate Service to an RTO, Pursuant to FERC-
Approved Rates, Terms, and Conditions in a FERC-Approved Tariff. 
The acute appellate risk presented by the IRAS Filing can be summarized by the 
following five sequential points: 
1. IRAS is a new wholesale rate service, subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the 
Commission, with rates, terms, and conditions established by the Commission 
under the Commission-approved PJM Tariff; 
2. PJM’s Tariff language makes clear that Eligible New Large Loads are the entities 
that provide IRAS as a wholesale rate service—not the Electric Distributor or Load 
Serving Entity; 
3. PJM’s Tariff language requires the mandatory and involuntary designation of 
Eligible New Large Loads to provide IRAS to PJM, and the compulsory provision 
of IRAS to PJM when called upon by PJM (through an implementing directive 
issued to the applicable Electric Distributor); 
4. Eligible New Large Loads have no contractual privity with PJM, are not subject to 
a FERC-jurisdictional load interconnection process, and are not public utilities 
under FPA section 201;12 and  
5. The FPA does not grant the Commission the legal authority to force end-use retail 
customers to be designated to provide a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service, 
or to compel the provision of that wholesale rate service, pursuant to a FERC-
approved Tariff. 
PPL Electric describes each of these five points in seriatim below, in subsections II.A.i-v. 
 
12 16 U.S.C. § 824.

6 
i. 
As proposed, IRAS is a new wholesale rate service, subject to the exclusive 
jurisdiction of the Commission, with rates, terms, and conditions established 
by the Commission under the Commission-approved PJM Tariff. 
As presented by PJM, IRAS is a new wholesale rate service, with rates, terms, and 
conditions established under the jurisdictional authority of the Commission.  This is axiomatic 
from the extensive Tariff and RAA revisions that PJM has submitted in this FPA section 205 
proceeding, covering everything from the definition of the service,13 eligibility requirements 
as to who can provide the service (Eligible New Large Loads),14 and the applicable rates for 
the service.15  Indeed, proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4 explicitly states that it “sets forth the 
terms and conditions governing the provision of Interim Resource Adequacy Service.”    
Moreover, the intended objective of IRAS is clear and unequivocal—“to maintain 
system reliability for the purpose of supporting the integration of New Large Loads to the PJM 
Region that are not in arrangements with new capacity additions to the PJM Region.”16  In 
other words, IRAS serves a fundamentally PJM-specific regional and FERC-centric purpose, 
and is not intended to fulfill any smaller state or local jurisdictional legal function under FPA 
section 201.   
Accordingly, as presented by PJM, IRAS is a new wholesale rate service, subject to the 
exclusive jurisdiction of the Commission, with its rates, terms, and conditions codified in the 
Commission-jurisdictional PJM Tariff. 
 
13 See Proposed Tariff, Definitions I-J-K (“Interim Resource Adequacy Service shall mean a load reduction 
service through which New Large Loads reduce load as directed by the applicable Electric Distributor in response 
to an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action requested by the Office of the Interconnection. Such reductions 
in load may be eligible for compensation pursuant to Attachment DD-4, section X.”). 
14 See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section V. 
15 Id. at Section X.  
16 Id. at Section I.

7 
ii. 
PJM’s Tariff language makes clear that Eligible New Large Loads are the 
entities that provide IRAS—not the Electric Distributor or Load Serving 
Entity. 
The Tariff language accompanying the IRAS Filing is unambiguous—Eligible New 
Large Loads (i.e., end-use retail customers) are the entities that “provide” IRAS as a FERC-
jurisdictional wholesale rate service. 
Eligible New Large Loads” shall mean a New Large Load 
eligible to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service in 
accordance with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section V.17 
Interim Resource Adequacy Service is a load reduction service, 
effective starting with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, through 
which Eligible New Large Loads may be compensated for 
providing load reductions requested by the Office of the 
Interconnection to maintain system reliability for the purpose 
of supporting the integration of New Large Loads to the PJM 
Region that are not in arrangements with new capacity additions 
to the PJM Region;18 
The Large Load Registry maintained by the Office of the 
Interconnection, pursuant to the Reliability Assurance 
Agreement, shall inform which New Large Loads are eligible 
to be called on to provide Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service;19  
The Office of the Interconnection Shall . . . determine the 
megawatt quantity of New Large Loads eligible to provide 
Interim Resource Adequacy Service in each Electric Distributor 
zone/area for a given Delivery Year.20 
All Eligible New Large Loads shall be available to be requested 
to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service by the Office of 
the Interconnection.21 
 
17 Proposed Tariff, Definitions E-F. 
18 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section I(a). 
19 Id. at Section I(c). 
20 Id. at Section II(c). 
21 Id. at Section IV(a).

8 
For purposes of removing its eligibility to provide Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service, a New Large Load may enter into 
arrangements with BYONC supported by one or more resources. 
While under PJM’s proposal, Electric Distributors and Load Serving Entities play an 
important role in “implementing” IRAS,22 they are not the entities actually “providing” IRAS 
as a wholesale, Commission-jurisdictional rate service to PJM.  This dynamic can be seen 
under PJM’s proposed compensation scheme as well, where the Eligible New Large Load is 
the entity entitled to compensation for providing IRAS service, notwithstanding that the 
Electric Distributor and state/local regulatory authorities can determine the implementation 
(and the ultimate applicability) of this compensation.23  
iii. 
PJM’s Tariff language requires the mandatory and involuntary designation 
of Eligible New Large Loads to provide IRAS to PJM, and the compulsory 
provision of IRAS to PJM when called upon by PJM (through an 
implementing directive issued to the applicable Electric Distributor). 
Under PJM’s proposed Tariff language, Eligible New Large Loads (i.e., end-use retail 
customers) are automatically designated as IRAS service providers by PJM.  In other words, 
designation as an entity that must provide FERC-jurisdictional wholesale IRAS service to PJM 
when called upon is mandatory, and this designation is made exclusively by PJM under its 
proposed Tariff language.   
(c) The Large Load Registry maintained by the Office of the 
Interconnection, pursuant to the Reliability Assurance 
Agreement, shall inform which New Large Loads are eligible 
to be called on to provide Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service.24 
 
22 See, e.g., id. at Section III(a) (“Electric Distributors shall . . . execute the Office of the Interconnection’s 
directives to implement Interim Resource Adequacy Service Actions among the Eligible New Large Loads in the 
Electric Distributor’s zone/area . .  .”).  See also id. at Section III(c) (“Electric Distributors shall . . . implement 
compensation program consistent with Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section X.”). 
23 See id. at Section X. 
24 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section I(c).

9 
All New Large Loads shall be Eligible New Large Loads to the 
extent that the sum of a New Large Load’s Eligible New Large 
Load Amount is less than the New Large Load’s registered 
peak load (in MW), as provided in the Large Load Registry. 
New Large Loads with a cumulative installed capacity 
equivalent of their BYONC arrangements and assigned 
Allocated RBP UCAP MW that equals or exceeds the New 
Large Load’s registered peak load, as provided in the Large 
Load Registry, shall not be Eligible New Large Loads. New 
Large Loads that are located within an FRR Service Area cannot 
be Eligible New Large Loads.25 
The Office of the Interconnection shall . . . identify Eligible 
New Large Loads.26 
While a New Large Load can theoretically reduce or eliminate its classification as an Eligible 
New Large Load and as an IRAS service provider via BYONC, this process too is exclusively 
determined pursuant to the terms and conditions of the FERC-jurisdictional PJM Tariff. 
For purposes of removing its eligibility to provide Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service, a New Large Load may enter into 
arrangements with BYONC supported by one or more 
resources.27 
Once designated as an Eligible New Large Load by PJM, PJM’s proposed Tariff 
language states that an Eligible New Large Load “shall” be available to provide IRAS when 
PJM sends out an implementing Operating Instruction to an applicable Electric Distributor.     
All Eligible New Large Loads shall be available to be requested 
to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service by the Office of 
the Interconnection. 
PJM explains that “in recognition of the jurisdictional divide between PJM and the states 
and/or RERRAs, PJM will not direct reductions to specific New Large Loads pursuant to 
 
25 Id. at Section V(a). 
26 Id. at Section II(b). 
27 Id. at Section V(c).

10 
IRAS,” but rather, “PJM is leaving it to Electric Distributors, in coordination with the 
appropriate states and/or RERRAs, LSEs, and LSE customers to determine which loads should 
ultimately reduce subject to IRAS.”28  This framing of the proposal’s jurisdictional challenges 
misses the point.  The issue is not about which entity gets to identify the specific individual 
Eligible New Large Loads that must provide IRAS when PJM calls for it.  The issue is that, 
when called upon to provide IRAS under that process, the Eligible New Large Load cannot 
say no.  It must, pursuant to a FERC-approved Tariff, provide IRAS as a FERC-jurisdictional 
wholesale rate service to PJM.  Put another way, the jurisdictional concern is not with the 
logistics of the “top-down,” directive to provide IRAS, but rather with the “bottom-up” 
requirement that IRAS be provided by the Eligible New Large Load when called upon by the 
Electric Distributor.  Or, as PJM describes it, “IRAS is a supplemental capacity product 
through which Eligible New Large Loads may be directed by the Electric Distributor to reduce 
their load in response to an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action called by PJM.”29 
Indeed, under PJM’s proposed Tariff language, the Electric Distributor is functionally 
little more than a conduit to implement PJM’s Operating Instruction.  This fact is built into the 
very definition of Interim Resource Adequacy Service, and Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service Action. 
“Interim Resource Adequacy Service” shall mean a load 
reduction service through which New Large Loads reduce load 
as directed by the applicable Electric Distributor in response to 
an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action requested by the 
Office of the Interconnection. Such reductions in load may be 
eligible for compensation pursuant to Attachment DD-4, section 
X.  
 
28 IRAS Filing at 92. 
29 Id. at 74.

11 
“Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action” shall mean an 
Operating Instruction, as defined by NERC, issued from the 
Office of the Interconnection to reduce load prior to calling on 
Pre-Emergency 
Load 
Management 
Reductions 
after 
determining that available economic real-time supply may not 
be sufficient to maintain reserves to meet applicable Reserve 
Requirements and/or Interconnection Reliability Operating 
Limits within prescribed limits and prevent cascading outages. 
While the Electric Distributor is the entity that is picking the specific individual Eligible 
New Large Loads to provide IRAS, it is simply a vehicle through which PJM “instruct[s] 
the implementation of an Interim Resource Adequacy Service Action.” 
Starting with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, the Office of the 
Interconnection may, in accordance with the Manuals, instruct 
the implementation of an Interim Resource Adequacy Service 
Action prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management 
Reductions Actions after determining that available economic 
real-time supply may not be sufficient to maintain reserves to 
meet applicable Reserve Requirements and/or Interconnection 
Reliability Operating Limits within prescribed limits and 
prevent cascading outages;30 
Electric Distributors shall:  
execute the Office of the Interconnection’s directives to 
implement Interim Resource Adequacy Service Actions among 
the Eligible New Large Loads in the Electric Distributor’s 
zone/area, which is an area within a Zone for which the relevant 
Electric Distributor specifies a separate Obligation Peak Load 
MW value and is a service area of an Electric Distributor that is 
a separately identifiable, geographic area bounded by wholesale 
metering;31 
This language does not solve the core jurisdictional problem, since the retail load is 
still being required to take action pursuant to an FPA jurisdictional tariff.  The obligation under 
 
30 Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section I(b). 
31 Id. at Section III(a).

12 
the tariff is not on the Electric Distributor, but forwarded onto its retail end-use customers (the 
Eligible New Large Loads) to provide the wholesale service under the tariff.   
iv. 
Eligible New Large Loads have no contractual privity with PJM, are not 
subject to a FERC-jurisdictional load interconnection process, and are not 
public utilities under FPA section 201. 
In many instances, Electric Distributors32 and Load Serving Entities33 are not public 
utilities by default, as defined in the FPA, and are therefore excluded from the Commission’s 
general rate and transmission jurisdiction under FPA section 201.34  These entities may 
nonetheless voluntarily agree to become subject to a multitude of obligations and requirements 
from PJM by virtue of signing the PJM Operating Agreement (for Electric Distributors) and 
RAA (for Load Serving Entities), which in addition to being FERC-filed tariffs,35 are also 
contracts.  This framework can also apply to end-use retail customers who choose to participate 
in PJM’s demand response market.  These entities are not jurisdictional public utilities solely 
 
32 Under the Operating Agreement, Electric Distributor means “a Member that: 1) owns or leases with rights 
equivalent to ownership electric distribution facilities that are used to provide electric distribution service to 
electric load within the PJM Region; or 2) is a generation and transmission cooperative or a joint municipal agency 
that has a member that owns electric distribution facilities used to provide electric distribution service to electric 
load within the PJM Region.”). 
33 Under the Operating Agreement, a Load Serving Entity is defined as “any entity (or the duly designated agent 
of such an entity), including a load aggregator or power marketer, (i) serving end-users within the PJM Region, 
and (ii) that has been granted the authority or has an obligation pursuant to state or local law, regulation or 
franchise to sell electric energy to end-users located within the PJM Region. Load Serving Entity shall include 
any end-use customer that qualifies under state rules or a utility retail tariff to manage directly its own supply of 
electric power and energy and use of transmission and ancillary services.”). 
34 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1) (“The Commission . . . shall not have jurisdiction . . . over facilities used in local 
distribution . . .”).  See also 16 U.S.C. § 824(f) (“No provision in this subchapter shall apply to, or be deemed to 
include, the United States, a State or any political subdivision of a State, an electric cooperative that receives 
financing under the Rural Electrification Act of 1936 or that sells less than 4,000,000 megawatt hours of 
electricity per year, or any agency, authority, or instrumentality of any one or more of the foregoing, or any 
corporation which is wholly owned, directly or indirectly, by any one or more of the foregoing, or any officer, 
agent, or employee of any of the foregoing acting as such in the course of his official duty, unless such provision 
makes specific reference thereto.”). 
35 18 C.F.R. § 35.2(c)(1) (“The term tariff as used herein shall mean a statement of (1) electric service as defined 
in paragraph (a) of this section offered on a generally applicable basis, (2) rates and charges for or in connection 
with that service, and (3) all classifications, practices, rules, or regulations which in any manner affect or relate 
to the aforementioned service, rates, and charges.”).

13 
by virtue of selling demand response into PJM’s markets.36  Nonetheless, they may voluntarily 
agree to take on obligations to PJM by becoming PJM Members and executing the Operating 
Agreement.  PJM is correct in its assessment that the Operating Agreement and RAA can and 
do create these obligations and requirements on entities that are otherwise excluded from the 
Commission’s general rate and transmission jurisdiction under FPA section 201.37  
Yet none of these traditional jurisdictional or contractual “hooks” are present under 
PJM’s IRAS proposal.  Eligible New Large Loads (i.e. end-use retail customers) are required 
to provide IRAS when commanded by PJM (through the Electric Distributor), yet these entities 
are not jurisdictional public utilities under FPA section 201 and have no contractual privity 
with PJM through which they have voluntarily agreed to assume the obligations associated 
with providing this service.  These entities have not agreed to undertake such obligations with 
PJM as a condition of their load interconnection, because the terms and conditions of service 
to end-use customers, including their connection to the system, lies solely within the purview 
of individual states and RERRAs, not PJM or FERC.  
 
36 See, e.g., EnergyConnect, Inc., 130 FERC ¶ 61,031 (2010) (“[W]here an entity is only engaged in the provision 
of demand response services, and makes no sales of electric energy for resale, that entity would not own or operate 
facilities that are subject to the Commission's jurisdiction and would not be a public utility that is required to have 
a rate on file with the Commission. While jurisdictional facilities may include contracts, memoranda and other 
records utilized in connection with jurisdictional sales, we do not regard agreements to provide services from only 
demand response resources to be jurisdictional facilities because they involve agreements to reduce demand, i.e., 
agreements not to purchase electric energy under certain circumstances, rather than agreements to sell electric 
energy at wholesale. Such agreements are not jurisdictional facilities that cause a seller to be a public utility.”). 
37 IRAS Filing at 46 (“Authority exists today in the Operating Agreement to require Electric Distributors to 
provide to PJM all System, accounting, customer tracking, load forecasting (including all load to be served from 
its System) and other data necessary or appropriate to implement or administer [the Operating Agreement], and 
the Reliability Assurance Agreement[.]”).  See also IRAS Filing at 81 (“Indeed, the Operating Agreement 
explicitly authorizes PJM to coordinate the curtailment or shedding of load, or other measures appropriate to 
alleviate an Emergency, in order to preserve reliability in accordance with NERC, or Applicable Regional Entity 
principles, guidelines and standards, and to ensure the operation of the PJM Region in accordance with Good 
Utility Practice and this Agreement where an “Emergency” is defined as a condition that requires implementation 
of emergency procedures as defined in the PJM Manuals.”).

14 
The absence of these jurisdictional and contractual “hooks” leads to only one possible 
outcome—PJM’s proposal would use the Commission’s general rate and transmission 
jurisdiction under FPA section 201 to directly impose requirements on entities that are 
excluded from that jurisdiction by the same statutory section, and have not voluntarily agreed 
to become subject to those requirements.  For the reasons described below in the next section, 
this is beyond the Commission’s legal authority under the FPA, and is not legally durable on 
appeal. 
v. 
The FPA does not grant the Commission the legal authority to force end-
use retail customers to be designated to provide a FERC-jurisdictional 
wholesale rate service, or to compel the provision of that wholesale rate 
service, pursuant to a FERC-approved Tariff. 
Simply put, in the IRAS Filing PJM is asking the Commission to do something that it 
is not statutorily permitted to do under the FPA.  As the D.C. Circuit has noted on more than 
one occasion, “as a federal agency, FERC is a creature of statute, having no constitutional or 
common law existence or authority, but only those authorities conferred upon it by 
Congress.”38  There is nothing in the FPA that grants the Commission the legal authority to 
force end-use retail customers (in this case, Eligible New Large Loads) to be designated to 
provide a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate service (IRAS), or to compel the provision of 
that wholesale rate service, pursuant to a FERC-approved tariff.  PJM cites to two primary 
legal authorities in support of the IRAS Filing, but as explained below, neither of these supports 
the action that PJM is suggesting the Commission take here. 
First, PJM cites to the Supreme Court’s ruling in EPSA, correctly noting that there “the 
Supreme Court held that the Commission’s regulation of demand response ‘addresses—and 
 
38 Atlantic City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 8 (D.C. Cir.2002) (quoting Michigan v. EPA, 268 F.3d 1075, 1081 
(D.C. Cir. 2001)).

15 
addresses only—transactions occurring on the wholesale market’ and takes aim at ‘enhanc[ing] 
the wholesale, not retail, electricity market.”39  PJM also correctly describes the Court’s 
holding that “the Commission’s rules for demand response withstood the Electric Power 
Supply Association’s jurisdictional challenge by respecting the division of federal/state 
authority set forth in the FPA.”40  Yet EPSA affirmed the Commission’s legal authority under 
the FPA to set the rates, terms, and conditions of voluntary wholesale demand response 
programs administered by RTOs.  EPSA is therefore inapposite to the proposition before the 
Commission under the IRAS Filing—the mandatory and involuntary designation of end-use 
retail customers (Eligible New Large Loads) to provide a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale rate 
service (IRAS) under the PJM Tariff, and the compulsory provision of that service pursuant to 
the rates, terms, and conditions of the PJM Tariff. 
Second, PJM similarly cites to the Commission’s 2025 ruling on the Midcontinent 
Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (“MISO”) Revised Expedited Resource Addition Study 
(“ERAS”) proposal41 for the proposition that placing the responsibility to determine which 
specific individual Eligible New Large Load will provide IRAS on PJM’s command with state 
and local regulatory authorities is “permissible and not an improper delegation of federal 
authority to the states.”42  PJM’s reliance on the MISO order is similarly misplaced.  As noted 
above, the jurisdictional concern is not with the logistics of the “top-down,” directive to 
provide IRAS, but rather with the “bottom-up” requirement that IRAS be provided by the 
Eligible New Large Load when called upon by PJM, through the Electric Distributor.  MISO’s 
 
39 IRAS Filing at 91 (citing EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282, 287).  
40 Id. (citing EPSA, 577 U.S. at 288-91). 
41 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,064 at P 99 (2025). 
42 IRAS Filing at 92.

16 
ERAS proposal created a framework for the expedited study of generator interconnection 
requests to address urgent, near-term resource adequacy and reliability needs.  It did not compel 
involuntary participation in that process.  Importantly, it was also focused on generator 
interconnection—an area that the Commission has clear jurisdiction over going back at least 
to Order No. 200343 and Tennessee Power.44  The Commission has never claimed such organic 
jurisdiction over retail load interconnection, which is the core problem that IRAS seeks to 
address. 
B. The IRAS Filing Contains Several Structural Deficiencies that Should Be Rejected 
or Modified under PJM’s NRG Invitation.  
i. 
Allowing Electric Distributors and state and local regulatory authorities to 
determine the wholesale rate paid for IRAS service is an impermissible 
delegation of the Commission’s wholesale rate-making authority under the 
FPA, and violates the Commission’s requirement under Part 35 that rates be 
stated “clearly and specifically” within a filed tariff. 
As referenced above, IRAS is a wholesale, FERC-jurisdictional service.  Yet PJM’s 
proposed Tariff language would turn over the ability to set and modify the rate paid for this 
wholesale service entirely to entities that do not have the legal authority to set and modify 
wholesale rates—Electric Distributors, and state and local regulatory authorities.  Specifically, 
PJM proposes a rate for IRAS that is equal to 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate, but 
notes that “the wholesale IRAS rate is flexible and can be further reduced to less than 50% of 
the Non-Performance Charge Rate if the Eligible New Large Load accepts in its retail rate a 
 
43 Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103 at P 12 (2003) 
(“Order No. 2003”) (“Interconnection is a critical component of open access transmission service, and standard 
interconnection procedures and a standard agreement applicable to Large Generators will serve several important 
functions.”). 
44 Tennessee Power Co., 90 FERC ¶ 61,238, 61,761-62 (2002) (“Tennessee Power”) (finding that interconnection 
is a critical component of open access transmission service and thus is subject to the requirement that utilities 
offer comparable service under the OATT.).

17 
sum less than 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate.”45  To this point, PJM explains that 
it “is not mandating how IRAS-directed load reductions are to be compensated,” but is instead 
“proposing a just and reasonable maximum rate for such service.”46  As PJM further explains, 
“given that the Electric Distributors, in accordance with state programs, will have identified 
the loads to be reduced, it is the responsibility of the Electric Distributor and its applicable 
state regulator to determine the appropriate compensation scheme.”47  According to PJM, 
under its proposal “[w]hether a specific New Large Load may be entitled to compensation for 
provision of IRAS will be determined by state authorities under state law or RERRA as may 
be applicable.”48 
This is impermissible under the FPA, where only the Commission may set and modify 
rates for wholesale services.  As the Court stated in EPSA, the FPA “leaves no room either for 
direct state regulation of the prices of interstate wholesales or for regulation that would 
indirectly achieve the same result.”49  The Court highlighted this fact again that very same year 
in Hughes, noting that “[a] State must [] give effect to Congress’ desire to give FERC plenary 
authority over interstate wholesale rates, and to ensure that the States do not interfere with this 
authority.”50  PJM’s proposal would not just allow states to “interfere” with FERC’s authority 
over interstate wholesale rates, it would delegate to states, local regulatory authorities, and 
Electric Distributors the ability to set and modify the interstate wholesale rate for IRAS,

46 Id. at 27. 
47 Id. at 28. 
48 Id. at 106. 
49 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 288 (citing N. Natural Gas Co. v State Corp. Comm’n of Kan., 372 U.S. 84, 91 (1963) 
(internal quotation marks omitted)). 
50 Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 164 (2016) (“Hughes”).

18 
including the ability to set the rate to $0.  To this point, PJM explains that the “IRAS rate is 
compensation for a wholesale load reduction service, but the entities to be paid the rate and the 
loads to be charged to support such compensation must be determined at the state level 
consistent with the Electric Distributor’s state-approved load reduction plans and other state-
approved programs, rates, and rules.”51  
Beyond this impermissible delegation, this compensation scheme also fails to meet the 
Commission’s regulations implementing FPA section 205(c), which are unambiguous—clarity 
and specificity are required when rates and charges are filed with the Commission. 
Every public utility shall file with the Commission and post, in 
conformity with the requirements of this part, full and complete 
rate schedules and tariffs and those service agreements not 
meeting the requirements of § 35.1(g), clearly and specifically 
setting forth all rates and charges for any transmission or sale 
of electric energy subject to the jurisdiction of this 
Commission, the classifications, practices, rules and regulations 
affecting such rates, charges, classifications, services, rules, 
regulations or practices, as required by section 205(c) of the 
Federal Power Act (49 Stat. 851; 16 U.S.C. 824d(c)).52 
The Commission has explained that an RTO has “[an] obligation to set forth its Commission-
jurisdictional rates clearly and specifically in its tariff.”53  The need to set forth rates and 
charges “clearly and specifically” is essential for the Commission’s own FPA section 205(c) 
analysis, as “[a] minimum level of specificity within the tariff is necessary for the Commission 
to determine whether the charges that result are just and reasonable.”54  It is also important in

particular FERC jurisdictional tariff, the state is setting the rate that is enforced under a federal tariff.  In either 
case, the state, not the public utility or FERC, is setting the FERC jurisdictional rate. 
52 18 C.F.R. § 35.1(a) (emphasis added). 
53 Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 112 FERC ¶ 61,009 at P 114 (2005).  
54 Id.

19 
fulfilling the fundamental purpose of FPA section 205(c) to provide notice to customers, as the 
requirement “allows [] customers the opportunity to assess for themselves whether they were 
properly charged.”55  Yet here, the wholesale rate paid or the charges imposed on funding 
customers from PJM’s proposed Tariff language in proposed Attachment DD-4, Section X, are 
unascertainable because the specific wholesale rate actually charged would be determined by 
entities wholly outside of the PJM Tariff.  Furthermore, the delegation of the wholesale rate 
setting function to Electric Distributors and state/local regulatory authorities would deny 
customers the protections afforded by FPA section 206.  If a customer viewed a charge for 
IRAS as too high, or not properly implemented, a complaint under FPA section 206 would be 
of little use, since the rate is being set outside of the PJM Tariff by entities other than the 
Commission, where FPA section 206 is legally incognizable. 
ii. 
PJM has not explained why it is appropriate to exclude New Large Loads 
from the VRR Curve to avoid charging customers, simultaneously charge 
those same customers in order to pay New Large Loads to provide IRAS, and 
deploy IRAS before demand resources for which customers have already been 
charged via the capacity market. 
Under the IRAS Filing PJM proposes to, beginning with the 2029/2030 Delivery Year, 
exclude from the demand curve (i.e., the VRR Curve used in RPM Auctions) the MW of New 
Large Loads that have not entered into BYONC arrangements or do not have Allocated RBP 
UCAP MW, over and above the MW of New Large Loads that were included in the load 
forecast for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.56  This, by definition, means that end-use retail 
customers (including the New Large Loads themselves) will receive the benefit of not being 
charged for the capacity necessary to support these New Large Loads.  However, these benefits 
 
55 Id. 
56 IRAS Filing at 109.

20 
are not sustained under PJM’s proposal since customers would be separately charged to 
compensate Eligible New Large Loads for providing IRAS.57  This concept stands out even 
more when considering that, according to PJM, IRAS will be deployed before demand 
resources that customers have already paid for via the capacity market.58  In other words, under 
PJM’s proposal: (i) customers (including New Large Loads themselves) will receive the 
benefit of not being charged for capacity by virtue of New Large Loads being excluded from 
the VRR Curve; (ii) customers will then be charged anyway in order to pay Eligible New Large 
Loads to provide IRAS; and (iii) PJM will deploy IRAS before calling demand resources, 
which customers have already paid for via the capacity market.  PJM has simply not justified 
why this approach is logically consistent from a policy perspective, much less just and 
reasonable under FPA section 205. 
iii. 
PJM’s Proposed Tariff Language Fails to Require Any Geographic Nexus 
Between BYONC Generation and the Load It is Intended to Offset, Which 
Will Shift Generation Constraints Into Transmission Constraints and Impose 
Additional Costs on Other Customers.   
PJM’s proposed BYONC provisions impose no requirement that generation supporting 
a BYONC arrangement be located in the same Locational Deliverability Area, Zone, or other 
defined geographic proximity to the New Large Load it is intended to offset.59  This issue was 
raised repeatedly during the Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) process, where the Joint EDCs 
and other stakeholders proposed various locational requirements for BYONC, but the PJM 
Board declined to adopt any such requirement.  As a Transmission Owner in PJM, PPL Electric 
is concerned that allowing BYONC generation to be sited anywhere on the system, without 
 
57 See Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section X. 
58 IRAS Filing at 74-75, 79. 
59 See id. at 23, 50-55.

21 
regard to its proximity to the load it offsets, will not eliminate resource adequacy risk so much 
as convert generation-related constraints into transmission-related constraints.  These 
transmission constraints must then be addressed via new transmission facilities that take years 
to plan, permit, and build, and the costs of which will ultimately be borne by other zonal 
customers.  PJM has failed to justify why these eminently foreseeable cost shifts under the 
IRAS Filing are just and reasonable under FPA Section 205. 
III. 
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION 
PPL Electric respectfully requests that PJM or the Commission provide clarification in 
this proceeding on several important components of the IRAS Filing.  
First, PPL Electric requests that PJM confirm on the record in this proceeding that it 
can in fact implement the mechanisms contemplated by the IRAS Filing between the requested 
effective date of October 26, 2026, and June 1, 2027, when IRAS would become available for 
use by PJM as a wholesale rate service.  Because so much of the IRAS Filing relies on 
cooperation among PJM’s fourteen distinct state jurisdictions and the diverse array of local 
regulatory authorities, Electric Distributors, and Load Serving Entities therein, this 
confirmation by PJM may very well help put these jurisdictions “on notice” as to the 
expectation and spur action to prepare.  PPL Electric remains concerned that this timeframe is 
simply too short for all of these external, non-PJM actors to stand up implementation regimes, 
but an “on-the-record” guidepost from PJM, the Commission, or both may help motivate at 
least some of these entities to seize the initiative and “meet the moment.”60 
Second, PPL Electric requests that PJM provide further detail in this proceeding 
regarding how RBP UCAP MWs will be allocated to a given zone for purposes of offsetting 
 
60 Supra note 6.

22 
IRAS responsibilities.  Under PJM’s proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IX, each 
Electric Distributor allocated RBP UCAP MWs must inform PJM of how RBP UCAP MWs 
should be further allocated among the New Large Loads located in the Electric Distributor’s 
zone/area.  However, in the event that the Electric Distributor has not informed PJM of how 
its RBP UCAP MWs should be further allocated by April 1 before a given Delivery Year, PJM 
must then allocate the RBP UCAP MWs to the Electric Distributor’s zone/area pro-rata among 
all New Large Loads located in the zone/area.  PPL Electric is concerned about the practical 
logistics of this proposal and the potential for inconsistency in allocation methods, given the 
extreme diversity among Electric Distributors and state/local regulatory authorities across the 
PJM Region.  Additional detail from PJM in this proceeding regarding its expectations and 
how it plans to deal with this contingency would be helpful as PPL Electric and other entities 
look to implementation.  
Third, PPL Electric requests clarification on the application of UCAP and ICAP in the 
context of BYONC.  While PJM proposes to define BYONC as “megawatts of Unforced 
Capacity that meet the eligibility criteria set forth in Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VI,”61 
PJM also notes that “the ICAP equivalent of this Accredited UCAP value is used to reduce a 
New Large Load’s potential IRAS availability.”62  PPL Electric is unclear from the IRAS 
Filing as to the reasoning for using these two different values in these two different contexts, 
and requests further explanation from PJM as to the implications of using these two very 
different values.   
 
61 Proposed Tariff, Definitions A-B. 
62 IRAS Filing at 65-66.

23 
Fourth, PPL Electric seeks clarity from PJM regarding the requirement in proposed 
Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section VII(e), which states that “BYONC that is in an arrangement 
with a New Large Load must remain in such arrangement with that New Large Load unless 
and until the New Large Load is permanently out-of-service.”  PPL Electric is unclear if the 
purpose of this provision is that a BYONC must stay in an arrangement with a New Large 
Load for the term of the contract underpinning the BYONC arrangement, or if the purpose of 
this provision is to force BYONC MWs to permanently be associated with that New Large 
Load.  It is also unclear if this obligation expires once BYONC has participated as a price taker 
for the first 10 years.  PPL Electric requests that PJM provide clarification on this point as well. 
Fifth, PPL Electric requests clarification regarding an apparent inconsistency between 
PJM’s proposed Tariff language and its transmittal letter description of the IRAS compensation 
scheme.  While the transmittal letter states that “it is the responsibility of the Electric 
Distributor and its applicable state regulator to determine the appropriate compensation 
scheme,”63 proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, Section X contains no reference to any Electric 
Distributor or state/RERRA role in setting or approving the compensation rate.  Rather, it 
addresses only a New Large Load’s own “election” to reduce or waive the applicable rate.64 
PPL Electric requests that PJM clarify how the state/RERRA role described in the transmittal 
letter is intended to be implemented under the actual proposed Tariff language, and, if that role 
is not reflected in the Tariff, that PJM revise proposed Section X accordingly. 
Finally, PPL Electric requests that PJM clarify whether and how PJM intends to address 
the transmission cost-shifting risk created by geographically unconstrained BYONC

arrangements, as noted above.  To this end, PPL Electric requests that PJM clarify whether it 
would consider adopting a preference, even short of a strict requirement, for geographic 
concentration between BYONC generation and the New Large Load it supports, given the 
transmission planning and cost allocations described above.  
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
Wherefore, for the foregoing reasons, PPL Electric respectfully requests that the 
Commission grant PPL Electric’s timely intervention in this proceeding and accept this Protest 
into the record.  PPL Electric also requests that either PJM or the Commission provide 
additional clarity regarding the items described above in Part III, and provide any additional 
guidance deemed appropriate.
